# Mechanical ventilation

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Pulmonology > Basics of pulmonology > Mechanical ventilation*

[Original Article Link](/library/xq0E0h)

---

## Summary

Mechanical ventilation is used to assist or replace spontaneous breathing to reduce the <u>work of breathing</u> and/or reverse life-threatening respiratory derangement in critically ill patients or to maintain respiratory function in those undergoing <u>general anesthesia</u>. It involves the application of positive pressure, which can be invasive (i.e., in intubated patients) or noninvasive (e.g., <u>CPAP</u> or <u>BiPAP</u>). Indications include <u>hypoxemic</u> and <u>hypercapnic respiratory failure</u>, hemodynamic compromise, and the need for close ventilatory control (e.g., therapeutic <u>hyperventilation</u>). Settings such as <u>ventilation modes</u> (e.g., assist-control, pressure-support) and parameters (e.g., <u>tidal volume</u>, <u>respiratory rate</u>, <u>FiO<sub>2</sub></u>, <u>PEEP</u>) should be adjusted to patient needs in order to minimize complications and restore <u>homeostasis</u>. A variety of <u>ventilation strategies</u> have been described for treating different types of <u>respiratory failure</u>. These should be implemented in a critical care setting with close monitoring in collaboration with specialists, nurses, and respiratory therapists. <u>Complications of mechanical ventilation</u> include <u>ventilator-induced lung injury</u> and <u>ventilator-associated pneumonia</u>, as well as extrapulmonary complications such as <u>GI ulcers</u> and <u>venous thromboembolism</u>. A systematic approach to common problems in mechanical ventilation (e.g., sudden deterioration, problems with oxygenation and ventilation, hemodynamic compromise, <u>patient-ventilator dyssynchrony</u>, <u>dynamic hyperinflation</u>) is recommended to prevent <u>morbidity</u> and mortality. Once patients show sufficient spontaneous breathing, they are weaned off ventilation support. See also <u>airway management</u>.

---

## Definitions

* Mechanical ventilation: use of a ventilator to assist or completely replace spontaneous breathing

---

## Positive-pressure ventilation

<u>Positive-pressure ventilation</u> (PPV) is the underlying mechanism of modern mechanical ventilators  [[1]](/library/PUbWWG)




* Definition: Oxygenated air is pushed into the <u>lungs</u> by a mechanical ventilation device that generates a positive pressure gradient. 

* Exhalation occurs through passive <u>elastic recoil</u>.

* May be administered invasively (e.g., via endotracheal or <u>tracheostomy</u> tube) or noninvasively (e.g., via a secured mask, as in <u>BiPAP</u> or <u>CPAP</u>)

* Effects of positive-pressure ventilation 

* Increased <u>airway</u> pressures

* Promotes <u>gas exchange</u> and recruitment/<u>stenting</u> of <u>alveoli</u>

* ↑ Risk of <u>ventilator-induced lung injury</u> (e.g., <u>barotrauma</u>)

* ↑ <u>Pulmonary artery</u> pressure

* ↑ <u>Pulmonary vascular resistance</u>

* Increased intrathoracic pressure → ↑ <u>pulmonary vascular resistance</u> and ↓ <u>venous return</u> → ↓ venous drainage of extrathoracic organs and ↓ <u>cardiac output</u> [[2]](/library/tPWXgl0)

* Right <u>heart</u>: ↓ <u>right atrium</u> filling, ↓ <u>right ventricle</u> (RV) <u>preload</u>, ↓ RV <u>stroke volume</u>, ↑ RV work, ↑ RV <u>afterload</u>

* Left <u>heart</u>: ↓ <u>left ventricle</u> (LV) <u>preload</u>, ↓ LV <u>stroke volume</u>, ↓ LV <u>afterload</u>, ↓ LV work

* Abdominal: ↑ gastric distension, ↑ risk of <u>vomiting</u>/<u>aspiration</u>, ↑ abdominal compartment pressure, ↓ organ <u>perfusion</u>





![Airway pressure in spontaneous breathing and mechanical ventilation](media/zugi764pfhkcxiv6wtg0slcg.jpg)

Airway pressure in spontaneous breathing and mechanical ventilation

## Noninvasive positive-pressure ventilation

### Types of <u>noninvasive positive-pressure ventilation</u> (<u>NIPPV</u>) [[3]](/library/3wYSir)




![Improving ventilation](media/small_61080e9bdb421.jpg)

Improving ventilation




#### Continuous positive airway pressure (<u>CPAP</u>)




* The ventilator delivers one constant <u>airway</u> pressure throughout the respiratory cycle (e.g., 5 cm H<sub>2</sub>O).

* Equivalent to providing <u>PEEP</u> without any other support

* Used in <u>hypoxemic respiratory failure</u>;  (e.g., <u>cardiogenic pulmonary edema</u>, <u>OSA</u>)





![Continuous Positive Airway Pressure (CPAP)](media/y069buc7vxl0e70gl3ac8afy.jpg)

Continuous Positive Airway Pressure (CPAP)




#### Bilevel positive airway pressure (BIPAP)




* The ventilator delivers two pressure levels and cycles between them.

* Expiratory positive airway pressure (<u>EPAP</u>): baseline pressure provided 
* Safe range: < 10–15 cm H<sub>2</sub>O

* Inspiratory positive airway pressure (<u>IPAP</u>): <u>EPAP</u> plus added inspiratory <u>pressure support</u> (<u>PS</u>) 
* Safe range: < 20–25 cm H<sub>2</sub>O

* If there is no added inspiratory <u>pressure support</u> (i.e., when <u>IPAP</u> = <u>EPAP</u>), then the <u>EPAP</u> setting is equivalent to <u>CPAP</u>.

* If there is added inspiratory <u>pressure support</u> (i.e., <u>IPAP</u> > <u>EPAP</u>), then <u>EPAP</u> is equivalent to <u>PEEP</u> (see <u>invasive mechanical ventilation</u>).

* Used in <u>hypercapnic respiratory failure</u> and <u>hypoxemic respiratory failure</u>





> [!TIP]
> <u>CPAP</u> only delivers one <u>airway</u> pressure, equivalent to <u>PEEP</u>. BIPAP cycles between two <u>airway</u> pressures and offers inspiratory <u>pressure support</u>.




![Biphasic Positive Airway Pressure (BIPAP)](media/ww9oixjq83ni03fcnnpw26ei.jpg)

Biphasic Positive Airway Pressure (BIPAP)




### Indications for NIPPV [[4]](/library/GtYBUI)[[5]](/library/duYoJI)




* Treatment of <u>respiratory distress</u> in patients with:

* Acute <u>COPD exacerbation</u> with <u>respiratory acidosis</u> (e.g., <u>pH</u> ≤ 7.35, <u>PaCO<sub>2</sub></u>> 45 mm Hg, RR > 20–24)

* <u>Cardiogenic pulmonary edema</u> (without <u>shock</u> or <u>ACS</u>)

* <u>Asthma exacerbations</u>: This is a controversial indication.

* Treatment of acute <u>respiratory failure</u> in patients with:

* <u>Immunocompromise</u> (e.g., solid organ and <u>bone marrow transplant</u>)

* Chest trauma

* Postoperative deterioration

* Bridging to <u>intubation</u> in patients with challenging <u>preoxygenation</u> (e.g., <u>ARDS</u>) [[6]](/library/MCYMsr)

* Bridging back to unassisted breathing

* <u>Weaning</u> from <u>invasive mechanical ventilation</u> in patients with acute <u>hypercapnic respiratory failure</u>

* Prophylactic use after planned <u>extubation</u> in patients at high risk for recurrent <u>respiratory failure</u>

* Patients with a <u>level of care</u> precluding <u>invasive mechanical ventilation</u>

* Patient with a <u>do-not-intubate order</u> [[3]](/library/3wYSir)

* Trial of therapy while the underlying disease is treated

* Temporizing measure to provide life support until the arrival of family/friends

* <u>Palliative therapy</u> for terminal cancer patients with <u>dyspnea</u>





### Contraindications for NIPPV [[7]](/library/HtYKUI)[[8]](/library/WuYPJI)




* Impaired/absent spontaneous breathing and/or patient not cooperative with <u>NIPPV</u>

* Cardiac or <u>respiratory arrest</u>

* Severe <u>encephalopathy</u> (<u>GCS</u> < 10)

* Uncontrolled <u>agitation</u>

* Impaired <u>airway</u> protection

* <u>Upper airway</u> obstruction

* Inability to clear respiratory secretions

* Severe <u>upper GI bleeding</u>

* High risk of <u>aspiration</u>  [[9]](/library/38YSmI)

* Impaired mask seal

* Facial trauma

* <u>Surgery</u>

* Deformity

* High risk of adverse effects from positive pressure

* Recent <u>upper airway</u> or upper gastrointestinal <u>surgery</u>

* <u>Hemodynamic instability</u> or <u>cardiac arrhythmia</u>





> [!WARNING]
> Uncontrolled <u>agitation</u> is a contraindication for <u>NIPPV</u>.




### Procedure [[3]](/library/3wYSir)[[5]](/library/duYoJI)[[8]](/library/WuYPJI)




The following steps are pertinent to adults newly requiring <u>NIPPV</u>. Stable patients continuing home therapy (e.g., <u>CPAP</u> for longstanding <u>OSA</u>) should be started on their preferred interface and baseline settings.




* Preparation

* Obtain baseline <u>ABG</u> if feasible.

* Make sure the patient is comfortable, alert, and in sitting position.

* Monitor <u>pulse oximetry</u>, blood pressure, <u>ECG</u>, <u>ABG</u>, exhaled <u>tidal volume</u>, and <u>respiratory mechanics</u>.

* Explain the procedure to the patient.

* Prepare for <u>intubation</u> in case respiratory and clinical status deteriorates.

* Choice of interface [[8]](/library/WuYPJI) 

* Oronasal mask

* Total-face masks

* Nasal mask or nasal pillows

* Helmet

* <u>NIPPV</u> settings [[5]](/library/duYoJI)

* BIPAP mode  [[3]](/library/3wYSir)

* Low-high approach: Start with low pressures and adjust upward as needed and tolerated.

* Start <u>EPAP</u> at 3–5 cm H<sub>2</sub>O.

* Start <u>IPAP</u> at 10 cm H<sub>2</sub>O.

* High-low approach: Start with high pressures and adjust downward as needed and tolerated.

* Start <u>EPAP</u> at 5–8 cm H<sub>2</sub>O.

* Start <u>IPAP</u> at 20–25 cm H<sub>2</sub>O.

* <u>CPAP</u> mode: Set <u>PEEP</u> to 5–12 cm H<sub>2</sub>O.

* Titrate <u>FiO<sub>2</sub></u> (between 30% and 50%) to the desired oxygenation target (e.g., <u>SpO<sub>2</sub></u> 88–92% for <u>COPD</u>).

* Monitoring and adjustments

* Initially administer <u>NIPPV</u> for 30–60 minutes.

* Titrate initial pressures (<u>PEEP</u>/<u>EPAP</u> and <u>IPAP</u>) to:

* ↓ <u>Work of breathing</u> and <u>dyspnea</u>

* ↓ <u>Respiratory rate</u>

* ↑ <u>Tidal volume</u>

* ↓ <u>Patient-ventilator dyssynchrony</u>

* Check <u>ABG</u> after 20–30 minutes.

* If <u>SpO<sub>2</sub></u> is low, increase <u>FiO<sub>2</sub></u> and <u>PEEP</u>/<u>EPAP</u>.

* If <u>PaCO<sub>2</sub></u> is high, increase <u>IPAP</u>.

* If patient's condition worsens  , prepare to switch to <u>invasive mechanical ventilation</u> (see <u>endotracheal intubation</u>).





> [!TIP]
> Do not delay <u>invasive mechanical ventilation</u> (e.g., <u>intubation</u>) if a patient's condition is worsening with <u>NIPPV</u>.




![image](media/qd6mqnvmuz7azwjtckszbidw.jpg)




### Complications [[8]](/library/WuYPJI)




* Air leaks

* <u>Aspiration</u> and potential <u>aspiration pneumonia</u>

* Ventilator-associated <u>lung injury</u>: <u>barotrauma</u> or <u>pneumothorax</u>

* Severe gastric distention that necessitates <u>NG tube insertion</u>

* <u>Skin</u> irritation, <u>abrasions</u>, and nasal bridge <u>ulceration</u>

* Mucus plugging

* <u>Mucosal</u> dryness

## Ventilator settings

### Basic ventilation parameters [[1]](/library/PUbWWG)[[3]](/library/3wYSir)[[10]](/library/35YSPp)[[23]](/library/OBYIa7)[[24]](/library/QUbu1G)[[25]](/library/kUbmWG)



1. * <u>Tidal volume</u> (V<sub>t</sub>): the volume of air delivered to or taken by the patient per breath

* Set by the clinician in volume-controlled modes (e.g., 8–12 mL/kg <u>ideal body weight</u>)

* Measured by the ventilator in pressure-controlled or pressure-supported modes (e.g., <u>PRVC</u> and <u>PSV</u>)
2. * <u>Respiratory rate</u> (RR): breaths taken or delivered per minute

* Set by the clinician in the absence of patient-initiated breaths (e.g., ∼ 10–15/min)

* Set by the patient in spontaneous breathing modes

* Commonly a combination of patient-triggered assisted breaths and a clinician-set backup RR
3. * Fraction of inspired oxygen (<u>FiO<sub>2</sub></u>): the fraction of oxygen (by volume) in the inspired air

* <u>FiO<sub>2</sub></u> of room air = 21%

* <u>FiO<sub>2</sub></u> up to 100% can be delivered in perfectly sealed <u>ventilator circuits</u>.
4. * Positive end-expiratory pressure (<u>PEEP</u>):

* Definition

* Positive pressure in the <u>lung</u> maintained over the entire inhalation and expiration phases

* Measured in centimeters of water (cm H<sub>2</sub>O)

* Also known as extrinsic <u>PEEP</u> (as it is applied to the patient by the device)

* Mechanism of action: keeps <u>airway</u> pressure above the atmospheric level at the end of exhalation → increases <u>alveolar pressure</u> and volume → reopens collapsed or unstable <u>alveoli</u> → improves ventilation/<u>perfusion</u> relation

* Indications: <u>PEEP</u> is typically justified when a <u>PaO<sub>2</sub></u> of 60 mm Hg cannot be achieved with an <u>FiO<sub>2</sub></u> of 60%.

* Almost all patients need a minimum amount of <u>PEEP</u> (3–5 cm H<sub>2</sub>O).

* Higher <u>PEEP</u> is indicated in conditions involving a <u>right-to-left pulmonary shunt</u> pathology.

* Advantages

* Prevent <u>atelectasis</u>

* ↑ Oxygenation without increasing the risk of <u>oxygen toxicity</u>

* ↑ <u>Gas exchange</u> area

* ↑ <u>Functional residual capacity</u>

* ↑ <u>Pulmonary compliance</u>

* Adverse effects

* <u>Ventilator-induced lung injury</u>

* <u>Patient-ventilator dyssynchrony</u>

* See “adverse effects” of <u>positive pressure ventilation</u>.

* See <u>hemodynamic compromise in mechanically ventilated patients</u>.




### Ventilator modes [[1]](/library/PUbWWG)[[3]](/library/3wYSir)[[10]](/library/35YSPp)[[23]](/library/OBYIa7)[[24]](/library/QUbu1G)[[25]](/library/kUbmWG)




#### Mandatory ventilation modes




Mandatory modes are useful when respiratory musculature is weak/paralyzed and <u>respiratory drive</u> is impaired.




* Examples

* Assist-control (AC) ventilation: can consist of <u>volume-control ventilation</u> (<u>VCV</u>) or <u>pressure-control ventilation</u> (<u>PCV</u>)

* <u>Pressure-regulated volume control</u> (<u>PRVC</u>)

* Description

* Breath frequency and waveforms are mostly controlled by the clinician.

* A minimum number of breaths per minute are delivered by the ventilator.

* Patients can trigger additional breaths above the minimum set rate.

* The breath volume and/or pressure are fixed and are independent of patient effort.





![The what and why of mechanical ventilation](media/small_6107fae215bff.jpg)

The what and why of mechanical ventilation

![Assist control (AC) and synchronized intermittent mandatory ventilation (SIMV) modes](media/small_6107f75dedcb0.jpg)

Assist control (AC) and synchronized intermittent mandatory ventilation (SIMV) modes

![Volume versus pressure control](media/small_6107f86d64c07.jpg)

Volume versus pressure control




#### Spontaneous ventilation modes




Spontaneous modes are useful for when respiratory musculature is intact/weak and <u>respiratory drive</u> is intact.




* Example: <u>pressure-support ventilation</u> (<u>PSV</u>)

* Description:

* Breath frequency and waveforms are mostly controlled by the patient.

* The ventilator only provides inspiratory pressure to support breathing.

* Almost all breaths are patient-triggered.

* Breath volume and duration depend on patient effort and the degree of inspiratory pressure provided.





#### Comparison of commonly used <u>ventilator modes</u>




| <br>Comparison of ventilator modes [[3]](/library/3wYSir)[[23]](/library/OBYIa7)[[24]](/library/QUbu1G)[[25]](/library/kUbmWG)<br> |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Mode | Programming | Advantages | Disadvantages |
| Volume-control ventilation (<u>VCV</u>) | <br><br>* Preset by clinician: V<sub>t</sub>, RR, <u>PEEP</u><br><br>* Ventilator delivers fixed volume.<br><br>* Variables to be monitored: inspiratory pressure<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Ideal as the initial mode of ventilation immediately after <u>intubation</u><br><br>* Allows strict control of <u>minute ventilation</u><br><br>* Allows guaranteed volumes to be delivered when <u>chest wall compliance</u> is low<br><br><br> | <br><br>* High <u>peak inspiratory pressures</u> may occur<br><br>* ↑ Risk of <u>VILI</u> in patients with poor <u>lung compliance</u><br><br>* ↑ Risk of <u>auto-PEEP</u> and <u>dynamic hyperinflation</u><br><br>* ↑ Risk of <u>hyperventilation</u> in patients with low sedation and high <u>respiratory drive</u><br><br><br> |
| <br>Pressure-control ventilation (<u>PCV</u>)<br> | <br><br>* Preset by clinician: inspiratory pressure limit, RR, <u>PEEP</u><br><br>* Ventilator delivers airflow at a fixed inspiratory pressure.<br><br>* Variables to be monitored: V<sub>t</sub><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Ideal for <u>obstructive lung diseases</u>  due to a reduced risk of developing <u>auto-PEEP</u> and <u>dynamic hyperinflation</u><br><br>* Ideal for conditions with ↑ <u>respiratory drive</u><br><br>* Allows precise adjustment of inspiratory time<br><br>* Reduces alveolar overdistention and risk of <u>VILI</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Volumes delivered are dependent on resistance and compliance in the circuit and can be unpredictable if these vary.<br><br>* Traditional alarms need to be adjusted to monitor volumes.<br><br><br> |
| Pressure-regulated volume-control (<u>PRVC</u>) | <br><br>* Hybrid of <u>VCV</u> and <u>PCV</u><br><br>* Preset by clinician: inspiratory pressure limit, target V<sub>t</sub>, RR, <u>PEEP</u><br><br>* Ventilator starts with <u>PCV</u> and adjusts inspiratory pressure breath-to-breath based on adaptive targeting of measured V<sub>t</sub>.<br><br>* Variables to be monitored: delivered V<sub>t</sub><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Combines the advantages of both <u>VCV</u> and <u>PCV</u><br><br>* Less frequent high <u>peak pressure</u> alarms than <u>VCV</u><br><br>* Less V<sub>t</sub> variability than <u>PCV</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Susceptible to disadvantages of both above modes.<br><br>* Patients with changes in <u>lung compliance</u> are still at risk of <u>VILI</u><br><br>* Can lead to <u>patient-ventilator dyssynchrony</u> if left unchecked [[26]](/library/oyY0T7)<br><br><br> |
| Pressure-support ventilation (<u>PSV</u>) | <br><br>* Preset by clinician: <u>IPAP</u>, <u>PEEP</u><br><br>* Ventilator adds inspiratory and expiratory pressure to support spontaneous breaths.<br><br>* Variables to be monitored: RR, V<sub>t</sub><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Ideal for <u>weaning</u><br><br>* Ideal for spontaneously breathing patients with healthy <u>lungs</u> who were intubated for <u>airway</u> protection<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Mandatory backup breaths in case of <u>apnea</u> are not automatic.<br><br>* <u>Hypoventilation</u> can occur in patients with reduced <u>respiratory drive</u> or changes in circuit compliance or resistance.<br><br><br> |





### Advanced settings



1. * Pressure support (<u>PS</u>): positive pressure added on top of <u>PEEP</u> during inspiration in pressure-supported <u>ventilation modes</u> (e.g., <u>PSV</u>) 

* Ranges from 5 cm H<sub>2</sub>O (minimal support) to 30 cm H<sub>2</sub>O (maximal support)

* <u>Work of breathing</u> is mostly accomplished by the ventilator if <u>PS</u> > 20 cm H<sub>2</sub>O.

* <u>PS</u> is typically increased to compensate for <u>respiratory muscle fatigue</u>, then gradually decreased during <u>weaning</u> from mechanical ventilation to allow patients to strengthen their respiratory musculature, with the goal of them breathing unassisted.
2. * <u>Peak inspiratory pressure</u> (<u>P<sub>IP</sub></u>) limit/target: preset parameter in pressure-controlled and pressure-regulated <u>ventilation modes</u> 

* In other <u>ventilator modes</u>, <u>P<sub>IP</sub></u> is a variable (see “monitoring” below).

* Typically set at ∼ 20–25 cm H<sub>2</sub>O to prevent <u>barotrauma</u>
3. * <u>Inspiratory flow rate</u> (VI): the rate of airflow sent into <u>lungs</u> during the inspiratory phase 
* Adjustable; flow rate typically set at at 60 L/min
4. * Inspiratory:expiratory ratio (<u>I:E ratio</u>): the <u>ratio</u> of inspiratory time to expiratory time in a given breathing cycle 

* Usually expressed in whole numbers (e.g., 1:2, 1:3)

* Can be adjusted directly or indirectly depending on the device

* Target <u>I:E ratios</u> are desirable in certain conditions (e.g., 1:4–1:5 for <u>obstructive lung disease</u>).

* Lower <u>I:E ratios</u> improve CO<sub>2</sub> clearance, minimize <u>air trapping</u> (<u>auto-PEEP</u>), and minimize the effect of positive-pressure on <u>hemodynamics</u>.

* Higher <u>I:E ratios</u> increase mean <u>airway</u> pressure and may enhance oxygenation and recruitment.

* Depends on other parameters

* ↑ RR→ ↓ time available for passive expiration → ↑ <u>I:E ratio</u>

* ↑ V<sub>t</sub> → ↑ time required for inspiration → ↑ <u>I:E ratio</u>

* ↑ VI → ↓ time required for inspiration → ↓ <u>I:E ratio</u>

* Inspiratory time = Vt/VI

* Expiratory time = [breath cycle time (1/RR) - inspiratory time]

* <u>I:E ratio</u> = inspiratory time/expiratory time
5. * Trigger sensitivity (mechanical ventilation): the threshold of inspiratory pressure or flow-gradient at which the ventilator identifies the patient's attempt to initiate a breath 

* Typically standard to the device (1–3 cm H<sub>2</sub>O)

* Not commonly adjusted by clinicians

* Low <u>sensitivity</u> helps to decrease <u>work of breathing</u>

* High <u>sensitivity</u> helps to decrease <u>oversensing</u> of breaths

---

## Monitoring

### General principles




All mechanically ventilated patients require close clinical, biomechanical, and laboratory monitoring in a critical care unit. This should include:




* One-to-one nursing care

* Continuous cardiac and <u>hemodynamic monitoring</u>

* Respiratory monitoring: Sensors can be externally applied or built into modern ventilators.

* Temperature monitoring

* <u>Blood gas analysis</u> monitoring





### External monitoring [[27]](/library/sBYtX7)




* <u>Pulse oximetry</u>

* Advantages

* Widely available and portable

* Easy to interpret in real-time

* High <u>accuracy</u> if <u>SpO<sub>2</sub></u> > 70%

* Disadvantages: not as accurate as <u>PaO<sub>2</sub></u>

* ↓ <u>Accuracy</u> in the case of: <u>hypovolemia</u>, <u>hypothermia</u>, <u>vasopressor</u> use, dyshemoglobinemia (e.g., <u>carboxyhemoglobin</u>, <u>methemoglobin</u>)

* Poor <u>sensitivity</u> for <u>hyperoxia</u>

* Capnometry (portable): numerical measurement of <u>end-tidal CO<sub>2</sub></u> (<u>EtCO<sub>2</sub></u>) [[28]](/library/F2bgjG)

* Description

* Externally-applied devices are being used with increasing frequency.

* Expired air is sampled through a tube.

* A transducer detects CO<sub>2</sub>and the amount is displayed on the monitor.

* Primary uses

* Determining the adequacy of ventilation

* <u>Confirming ET tube placement</u>

* RR monitoring

* Secondary uses

* Short term guidance of <u>hyperventilation</u> therapy (e.g., treating <u>↑ ICP</u>)

* Diagnosing <u>pulmonary embolism</u>

* Preventing <u>hypercapnia</u>, e.g., in <u>brain</u>-injured and post-<u>cardiac arrest</u> patients

* Assessing <u>CPR</u> quality

* Disadvantages: underestimates <u>PaCO<sub>2</sub></u> compared to <u>ABG</u>

* Advanced monitoring to consider: especially for conditions exacerbated by <u>positive pressure ventilation</u>.

* <u>Hemodynamically unstable</u> patients: <u>CVP</u> monitoring; <u>IVC</u> diameter and collapsibility

* Patients at risk of <u>abdominal compartment syndrome</u>: abdominal compartment pressures





![Anesthesia monitor](media/fmdbp9eqs3e3mua0b69hmoz3.jpg)

Anesthesia monitor




### Ventilator-based monitoring [[3]](/library/3wYSir)[[10]](/library/35YSPp)[[27]](/library/sBYtX7)




The following are standard measurements built into most newer generation ventilators.




#### Capnography




* Description

* Waveform version of <u>capnometry</u> displaying CO<sub>2</sub> measurements in exhaled air over time

* The <u>EtCO<sub>2</sub></u> is measured at the end of the expiratory phase of the breathing cycle.

* Sensors are typically integrated into the ventilator but can be portable in rare cases.

* Interpretation

* Normal waveform: rapid increase of the CO<sub>2</sub> concentration → plateau → rapid decrease in the CO<sub>2</sub> concentration during inspiration.

* Loss of waveform

* <u>Cardiac arrest</u>

* Accidental <u>extubation</u>

* Complete tube obstruction

* Significant decrease in waveform amplitude

* Partial tube obstruction

* <u>Airway</u> leak

* <u>Hypotension</u>





#### Pressure monitoring [[13]](/library/FBYgc7)[[29]](/library/QAYuj7)




* Peak inspiratory pressure (<u>P<sub>IP</sub></u>):

* Definition: the maximum pressure measured at any point throughout the inspiratory phase

* Description: primarily reflects <u>airway resistance</u>; <u>lung compliance</u> reflected to a lesser degree

* <u>VCV</u>

* Measured <u>P<sub>IP</sub></u> is greatly influenced by <u>airway resistance</u>.

* Less reflective of <u>alveolar pressure</u> and risk of <u>VILI</u>

* <u>PCV</u>/<u>PRVC</u>

* <u>P<sub>IP</sub></u> = inspiratory pressure target + <u>PEEP</u>

* Accurately reflects <u>alveolar pressure</u> and correlates well with <u>VILI</u> risk

* Interpretation: <u>P<sub>IP</sub></u> > 35–40 cm H<sub>2</sub>O is generally considered elevated.

* Plateau pressure (<u>P<sub>Plat</sub></u>)

* Definition: the maximum air pressure measured during a pause at the end of inspiration

* Description: reflects <u>lung compliance</u>
* <u>VCV</u>: more accurately reflects <u>alveolar pressure</u> and risk of <u>VILI</u> than <u>P<sub>IP</sub></u>

* Interpretation: P<sub>plat</sub>> 30 cm H<sub>2</sub>O is considered elevated.

* Auto-PEEP (<u>intrinsic PEEP</u>) [[30]](/library/YyYnd7)

* Definition: <u>PEEP</u> remaining in the circuit at the end of expiration that is not delivered by the ventilator, i.e., generated by the patient

* Description

* Tends to occur in conditions in which the expiratory outflow is impaired (e.g., <u>asthma</u>)

* Expiration is incomplete at the end of a breath cycle → <u>air trapping</u> → <u>dynamic hyperinflation</u>

* Estimated using expiratory hold maneuver

* The circuit is paused for 3–5 seconds at the end of expiration.

* The change in pressure waveform back to baseline is measured as it reaches equilibrium in the circuit, which is the total <u>PEEP</u>.

* <u>Auto-PEEP</u> = total <u>PEEP</u> - extrinsic <u>PEEP</u>

* Interpretation:

* Ideally, no <u>auto-PEEP</u> should be present.

* The presence and degree of <u>auto-PEEP</u> correlates with a higher risk of complications (e.g., <u>dynamic hyperinflation</u>, adverse effects of <u>positive pressure ventilation</u>).





![image](media/mxpp3pye7eo8gu1krvzepg8l.jpg)




### Laboratory monitoring [[31]](/library/7BY4X7)




#### Arterial blood gas monitoring




* General considerations

* More accurate than <u>pulse oximetry</u> for assessing oxygenation

* Essential for calculation of <u>P/F ratio</u>

* Consider an <u>arterial line</u> for patients requiring frequent arterial sampling.

* Normal physiological/compensated ranges are typically desirable (exceptions include <u>permissive hypercapnia</u>).

* Sampling frequency

* Within 30 minutes of <u>intubation</u>

* Within 1 hour of changes in <u>ventilator settings</u> or patient status

* Every 8–24 hours otherwise

* Interpretation: See also <u>arterial blood gas analysis</u>.

* Ventilation: <u>pH</u>, <u>PaCO<sub>2</sub></u>, HCO<sub>3</sub>

* <u>Respiratory acidosis</u> pattern: insufficient <u>minute ventilation</u>

* <u>Respiratory alkalosis</u> patterns: <u>iatrogenic</u> <u>hyperventilation</u>

* <u>Metabolic acidosis</u>/<u>alkalosis</u> patterns: Consider adjusting <u>minute ventilation</u> for compensation.

* See <u>improving ventilation in mechanically ventilated patients</u>.

* Oxygenation: <u>PaO<sub>2</sub></u>
* For interventions, see <u>improving oxygenation in mechanically ventilated patients</u>.





| Interpretation of oxygenation using <u>ABG</u> in mechanically ventilated patients |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Condition |  | <u>PaO<sub>2</sub></u> (mm Hg) |
| <u>Hypoxemia</u> |  | <br> < 70<br> |
| <u>Normoxemia</u> |  | 70–120 |
| <br><u>Hyperoxia</u>  [[32]](/library/mAYV47)[[33]](/library/5AYi47)<br> | Mild | 121–200 |
| Moderate | 201–300 |  |
| Severe | <br> > 300<br> |  |





#### <u>Venous blood gas</u> [[10]](/library/35YSPp)




* Generally correlates well with <u>ABG</u> for <u>pH</u>

* <u>Venous PCO<sub>2</sub></u> is not as reliable as <u>capnography</u>.

* Venous PO<sub>2</sub>is not as reliable as <u>pulse oximetry</u>.

## Complications

### Ventilator-induced lung injury (<u>VILI</u>) [[3]](/library/3wYSir)[[27]](/library/sBYtX7)




<u>VILI</u> refers to both pulmonary and extrapulmonary injuries resulting from any combination of the following.




* <u>Pulmonary barotrauma</u> [[34]](/library/YAYnR7)

* Mechanism: excess pressure in circuit → ↑ extra-alveolar air dissecting into other fascial planes and compartments

* Aggravating factors

* ↑ <u>PEEP</u>

* ↓ <u>Lung compliance</u>

* ↑ <u>Airway resistance</u>

* ↑ <u>Inspiratory flow rate</u>

* Consequences

* <u>Pneumothorax</u> and/or <u>tension pneumothorax</u>

* <u>Pneumomediastinum</u>

* <u>Pneumoperitoneum</u>

* <u>Subcutaneous emphysema</u>

* Volutrauma

* Mechanism: excess volume delivered → alveolar overdistention → disruption of alveolar-<u>capillary</u> membrane → release of inflammatory mediators

* Aggravating factors: ↑ V<sub>t</sub> and ↓ <u>lung compliance</u>

* Atelectrauma

* Mechanism: repeated opening and closing of <u>alveoli</u> (i.e., <u>atelectasis</u>) → shear <u>stress</u> → release of inflammatory mediators

* Aggravating factors: ↓ <u>PEEP</u> , ↓ V<sub>t</sub>, ↓ <u>pulmonary surfactant</u>

* Biotrauma

* Mechanism: release of inflammatory mediators from <u>lung</u> → systemic organ dysfunction

* Aggravating factors: <u>volutrauma</u>, <u>atelectrauma</u>

* <u>Oxygen toxicity</u> [[32]](/library/mAYV47)[[33]](/library/5AYi47)

* Mechanism: excess oxygen concentration → <u>free radical</u> formation, causing direct tissue injury (e.g., diffuse alveolar damage, tracheobronchitis) [[13]](/library/FBYgc7)

* Aggravating factor: ↑ <u>FiO<sub>2</sub></u>

* Consequences: <u>Hyperoxia</u> is associated with higher mortality in critically ill patients than <u>normoxemia</u>.





### Other complications




#### Intrapulmonary




* <u>VAP</u>: See “<u>Prevention of ventilator-associated infections</u>” and “<u>Empiric antibiotic therapy for ventilator-associated pneumonia</u>.”

* Inspiratory <u>muscle weakness</u> and <u>deconditioning</u> [[35]](/library/xAYEN7)

* Ventilator-associated <u>pulmonary fibrosis</u>: occurs in the subacute phase of <u>ARDS</u> [[36]](/library/1AY2i7)[[37]](/library/WAYPi7)





#### Extrapulmonary [[27]](/library/sBYtX7)




* Gastric <u>mucosal</u> injury (e.g., <u>PUD</u>, <u>GI bleed</u>)

* <u>Venous thromboembolism</u>  [[27]](/library/sBYtX7)

* Systemic <u>deconditioning</u>

* <u>Pressure ulcers</u>

* <u>Contractures</u>





We list the most important complications. The selection is not exhaustive.
